name: Daria Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paulo and I run Two Wells, a goat dairy with about 250 milking goats, plus maize and lucerne for feed and a farm shop where we sell our own cheese. We bought it eight years ago, with a mortgage and everything we'd saved from working on other people's farms. There are four staff: two in the cheese room, Marisol in the shop, and young Jake on the farm. We've got two kids, Clara who's fourteen and Tomás who's eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five for milking on the rotary, and the system reads each goat's tag and logs her milk before I've had coffee. After that I check the dashboards, plan the cheese batches, and use an AI assistant to write the shop newsletter, answer online orders and spot trends in what sells. Afternoons I'm in the fields or the shop, chatting to customers, which I love. What wears me out is red tape: food safety forms, planning rules for the shop extension, the council's way of saying no slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool and some people oversold it, as always happens in a market. I'd probably post in the cheesemakers' group about how it helped us, without the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, things stay good. We'd keep using the tools we've got, keep growing the shop, and the business keeps ticking over. Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed, I like a bit of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are. Use the AI tools for the shop and the orders, maybe add a better stock system. Keep saving for the shop extension, about 40 thousand, which I've been planning for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What would you miss in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea that we could do even more, maybe sell abroad, without hiring a whole office. In this picture I'd still be writing the export forms myself at ten at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gets the blame when the hype falls flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. People invested, some won, some lost. That's how markets work and it's fair enough. The government will probably try to regulate it anyway, which is the last thing we need.

S0.say: I'd say it was a useful tool that some people oversold, as always happens in a market. I'd post in the cheesemakers' group about how it helped us, without the hype.
S0.think: For me things stay good: we keep the tools we have, grow the shop and the business ticks over. I'd be a little disappointed, because I like a bit of change.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for the shop and online orders and adds a better stock system. Keeps saving for the 40 thousand shop extension she's planned for two years.
S0.quote: In this picture I'd still be writing the export forms myself at ten at night.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is a confident small business owner who already runs on data and AI tools. She talks in market terms and dislikes regulation. Her mild disappointment comes from wanting room to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for small business, if the government stays out of the way. The people who get on with it will be fine. I'd say it at the farmers' market and in the cheesemakers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's great for us. We're small, we move fast, and we already use the tools. The big dairies will be slow and we'll be ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot for turning and brushing the cheeses in the ripening room, about 30 thousand, and an AI system to plan the herd breeding. I'd open an online shop with proper delivery, using the time we save. And I'd go ahead with the farm shop extension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited. I'd be sketching the new cheese room on the back of an envelope that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change first at Two Wells?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cheese room. Turning cheeses is slow, heavy work that wrecks your wrists. A robot can do that and my two cheesemakers can do the creative part, new recipes, tastings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your four staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep all four, and move them up into better work. Marisol could run the online shop. Jake could manage the robots. That's the apprentice way, you train people up, you don't throw them out.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for small business if the government stays out of the way. People who get on with it will be fine, and I'd say so at the farmers' market.
S1.think: It's great for us, because we're small, we move fast and we already use the tools. The big dairies will be slow and we'll be ahead.
S1.do: Buys a cheese-turning robot for about 30 thousand and an AI breeding planner, then opens an online shop with delivery. Goes ahead with the farm shop extension and moves her four staff into new roles.
S1.quote: That's the apprentice way, you train people up, you don't throw them out.
S1.fieldNote: Daria sees steady disruption as an opening for small, fast businesses like hers. She'd invest quickly but keep and train her staff, which she ties to her belief in apprenticeships. She wants government to stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, but people should pull together, families and churches and neighbours, and not wait for the state to fix it. I'd say businesses that move fast will keep people working. I'd say that at Mass and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, our farm would be fine, I'd automate quickly. The worry is the customers. If nobody has wages, who buys forty-pound cheese boards at Christmas?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy robots for the milking parlour and the fields within six months, before prices jump. I'd keep a year's running costs in cash. And I'd cut the luxury lines and push cheaper everyday cheese, because that's what people will still buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the farm, about the people round us, the regulars who come in every Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. Is there anything that worries you about that speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the speed. Markets need time to adjust, and two years isn't enough. Prices would go haywire and people would panic before they figured out new ways to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Clara and Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're blessed and we'll be fine, but we have to help others. And I'd tell them to work hard at whatever's still needed, because there's always something.

S2.say: I'd say it will be rough, but families, churches and neighbours should pull together and not wait for the state. Businesses that move fast will keep people working, and I'd say so at Mass and online.
S2.think: Our farm would be fine because I'd automate quickly. The worry is the customers, because if nobody has wages, who buys cheese boards at Christmas?
S2.do: Buys robots for the parlour and fields within six months, before prices rise, and keeps a year's running costs in cash. Cuts luxury lines and pushes cheaper everyday cheese.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not about the farm but about the people around her.
S2.quote: If nobody has wages, who buys forty-pound cheese boards at Christmas?
S2.fieldNote: Daria's adaptability and ownership protect the farm itself, but she quickly sees that her customers' incomes are the weak point. Her response is market-minded: shift to cheaper products. She calls for community and church support rather than state help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can see it coming, so businesses should plan, invest, and keep people working where they can. I'd say families should prepare too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to do it well. We'd automate in stages and grow the business, maybe even buy the farm next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd automate the cheese room and start the online shop. Years two and three, I'd add field robots and buy the neighbour's 60 acres if it comes up. I'd keep training the staff for the new roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. This is the version I'd pick, if anyone asked me to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd stay, in new jobs. Jake runs the robots, Marisol runs the online side and the shop. I'd pay for their training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Jake and Marisol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And I'd start a cheese school, weekend courses for townies. People will have time, and they'll want to make things with their hands.

S3.say: I'd say we can see it coming, so businesses should plan, invest and keep people working where they can. Families should prepare too.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to do it well. We'd automate in stages, grow the business and maybe buy the farm next door.
S3.do: Automates the cheese room and starts the online shop in the first year, then adds field robots and buys the neighbouring 60 acres if they come up. Pays for staff training and starts weekend cheese-making courses.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, this is the picture she'd choose.
S3.quote: People will have time, and they'll want to make things with their hands.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Daria grow on her own terms, buying land and starting a cheese school. She keeps her staff and pays for their training. Her plans are confident and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway. Businesses and families can plan, and the state should keep its hands off as much as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. The farm keeps going, the robots do the heavy work, and I do what I like: the cheese, the customers, the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd pay down the mortgage faster and set aside money for robots. In a few years I'd buy them as they get cheaper. And I'd plan the kids' futures with them, maybe Clara takes on the cheese side one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even, the way I feel when the first kids are born in February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids. If machines do everything, I'd worry they never learn to work hard. Paulo and I both started at fourteen. I'd want them to know what that feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about, even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So they'd still have jobs on the farm, robots or not. Clara in the cheese room, Tomás with the goats. That's not optional in our house.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a good runway for businesses and families to plan. The state should keep its hands off as much as possible.
S4.think: I'd be fine: the farm keeps going, the robots do the heavy work and I do what I like, the cheese, the customers and the shop.
S4.do: Pays the mortgage down faster and sets money aside for robots, buying them as they get cheaper. Plans the children's futures with them, perhaps with her daughter taking on the cheese side.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with a worry that her children won't learn to work hard.
S4.quote: If machines do everything, I'd worry they never learn to work hard. Paulo and I both started at fourteen.
S4.fieldNote: Daria is secure and hopeful with a decade to plan. Her only worry is about her children's character, not money. She'd keep them working on the farm whatever robots can do, which fits her traditional values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but for our customers, not for us. What would help is the government cutting red tape so small businesses can move fast and keep people working, and families and churches looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the goats. They each have a personality. Sweet Pea headbutts the gate every morning till I let her out. A robot can milk her, but it won't laugh at her.

headlineQuote: A robot can milk her, but it won't laugh at her.
portrait: Daria Santos is a 43-year-old farmer who runs Two Wells, a goat dairy with a farm shop and cheese room, with her husband Paulo, two children and four staff. She uses AI tools every day, already milks on an automated rotary and talks in market terms, with little patience for red tape. She stays calm in most pictures and would automate fast while training her staff into new roles. AGI by 2028 makes her uneasy only because her customers might lose their wages. With more time, she plans to grow, start a cheese school and keep her children working on the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of what it would do to her customers' incomes rather than to her own farm.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape so small businesses can move fast and keep people working, and families and churches looking after each other.
